examMarks.basis: Chapter 1 questions in the 2022, 2023 and 2025 papers: 9, 7 and 7 marks

stops.title: Circular motion basics
stops.inShort: Revolution is motion about a point outside the body; rotation is about an axis through it. Circular motion is accelerated and periodic. v = ωr, ω = 2π/T = 2πn, and in UCM the centripetal acceleration is v²/r = ω²r towards the centre.

cards.text: Revolution is motion about a point outside the body; rotation is motion about an axis that passes through the body. Circular motion is accelerated, because the direction of velocity changes at every instant, and it is periodic.
The tangential (linear) speed of a particle is v = ωr, where ω is the angular velocity and r the radius. With period T and frequency n, ω = 2π/T = 2πn.
In uniform circular motion (UCM) the speed is constant but the direction of velocity keeps changing. The acceleration is centripetal, a_{r} = v²/r = ω²r, always directed towards the centre.

checks.q: Which statement about uniform circular motion (UCM) is correct?
options: The velocity is constant because the speed is constant
The speed is constant, but the velocity changes direction every instant, so there is a centripetal acceleration
The acceleration is zero because the speed does not change
The acceleration is along the direction of the velocity
checks.hint: Velocity is a vector. Ask whether its direction stays the same.
checks.explain: In UCM the speed is constant but the direction of velocity changes at every instant, so the motion is accelerated. The acceleration is centripetal: a_{r} = v²/r = ω²r, towards the centre.

checks.q: A wheel turns at 3 revolutions per second. Find its angular velocity ω.
checks.hint: Use ω = 2πn, where n is the frequency in revolutions per second.

checks.q: Rotation is motion about an axis passing through the body, while revolution is motion about a point or axis outside the body.
checks.hint: Think of a spinning top compared with the Earth going round the Sun.
checks.explain: That is exactly the textbook distinction: rotation is about an axis through the object, revolution is about a point outside it.

stops.title: Dynamics of circular motion
stops.inShort: A centripetal force mv²/r must be supplied by real forces (tension, friction, gravity, normal reaction). Centrifugal force is a pseudo force felt only in the rotating frame.

cards.text: For a body moving in a circle, the resultant of all the real forces on it points towards the centre. This resultant is the centripetal force, F = mv²/r = mω²r.

cards.t: Centripetal is not a new force
cards.text: 'Centripetal' tells you the direction of the force (towards the centre); it is not a separate type of force like gravity. Real forces such as tension, friction, weight or the normal reaction supply it, so do not add it as an extra force.
Centrifugal force mω²r, directed away from the centre, is a pseudo force. It is used only in the rotating frame of reference, where it balances the resultant real force.

checks.q: A stone is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string. What supplies the centripetal force?
options: A separate force called centripetal force
checks.hint: Which real force acts along the string towards the centre?
checks.explain: The centripetal force is the resultant of the real forces towards the centre. Here the tension in the string provides it.

checks.q: A 0.2 kg ball moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m with a speed of 5 m/s. Find the centripetal force.
checks.hint: Use F = mv²/r.

checks.q: Centrifugal force is a real force acting on the body, as seen from an inertial frame.
checks.hint: Is it present in the inertial frame, or only in the rotating frame?
checks.explain: Centrifugal force is a pseudo force. It appears only in the rotating (non-inertial) frame of reference.

stops.title: Car on a flat curved road
sections: 1.3.1 Vehicle Along a Horizontal Circular Track
stops.inShort: On a level curve, static friction supplies the centripetal force. Maximum safe speed: v = √(μs r g).

cards.text: On a level circular track the weight mg is balanced by the normal reaction N. The force of static friction between tyres and road is the centripetal force: f_{s} = mv²/r. It is static friction because it stops the car skidding outwards.
Static friction has an upper limit f_{s(max)} = μ_{s}N = μ_{s}mg. Putting this equal to mv²/r gives the maximum safe speed v_{max} = √(μ_{s}rg).
The mass cancels, so v_{max} does not depend on the mass of the vehicle. A larger radius or a rougher road (larger μ_{s}) allows a higher speed.

checks.q: A car takes a flat circular turn of radius 40 m. The coefficient of static friction is μ_{s} = 0.4. Find the maximum safe speed. (g = 10 m/s²)
checks.hint: v_{max} = √(μ_{s}rg).

checks.q: On a flat road with the same μ_{s}, a driver wants to double the safe speed. By what factor must the radius of the turn increase?
checks.hint: v_{max}² = μ_{s}rg, so how does r depend on v²?
checks.explain: v_{max}² = μ_{s}rg means r is proportional to v². Doubling v needs r to become 2² = 4 times.

checks.q: A car moves on a flat circular road at the limiting speed. Which equation do you write first?
checks.hint: Which force is the centripetal force on a flat road, and what is its largest value?
checks.explain: On a flat road static friction supplies the centripetal force. At the limit, f_{s(max)} = μ_{s}N = μ_{s}mg equals mv²/r.

stops.title: Well of death
stops.inShort: The wall's normal reaction gives the centripetal force and friction holds the rider up against gravity. Minimum speed: v = √(r g / μs).

cards.t: Forces in the well of death
cards.text: The rider moves in horizontal circles on the inside of a vertical cylindrical wall of radius r. The forces are the normal reaction N (horizontal, towards the centre), the weight mg (down) and static friction f_{s} (up along the wall).
Horizontally, N = mv²/r is the centripetal force. Vertically, friction balances the weight, f_{s} = mg. Since f_{s} ≤ μ_{s}N, we need mg ≤ μ_{s}mv²/r.
This gives the minimum speed v_{min} = √(rg/μ_{s}). Below it, N is too small for friction to hold the rider up against gravity.

checks.q: A motor cyclist rides horizontal circles inside a well of radius 4 m. The coefficient of static friction between tyres and wall is 0.4. Find the minimum speed. (g = 10 m/s²)
checks.hint: v_{min} = √(rg/μ_{s}).

checks.q: In the well of death, which force balances the weight of the rider?
checks.hint: The weight acts vertically down. Which force acts vertically up along the wall?
checks.explain: The normal reaction is horizontal and gives the centripetal force. The upward force along the wall is static friction, f_{s} = mg.

checks.q: If the coefficient of static friction μ_{s} increases, the minimum speed needed in the well of death also increases.
checks.hint: Look at v_{min} = √(rg/μ_{s}): μ_{s} is in the denominator.
checks.explain: v_{min} = √(rg/μ_{s}), so a larger μ_{s} gives a smaller minimum speed.

stops.title: Banked road
stops.inShort: Banking tilts the normal reaction so its horizontal part supplies the centripetal force. Most safe speed without friction: v = √(r g tanθ). With friction there is a maximum and a minimum safe speed.

cards.text: On a road banked at angle θ the normal reaction N is tilted. Its vertical part balances the weight, N cosθ = mg, and its horizontal part is the centripetal force, N sinθ = mv²/r. Dividing gives tanθ = v²/(rg).
The most safe speed is v_{s} = √(rg tanθ), and the angle of banking is θ = tan⁻¹(v²/rg). It is the speed at which no friction is needed.
With friction there are limits: v_{min} = √(rg(tanθ − μ_{s})/(1 + μ_{s}tanθ)) and v_{max} = √(rg(tanθ + μ_{s})/(1 − μ_{s}tanθ)). For μ_{s} = 0 both reduce to √(rg tanθ).

checks.q: A frictionless road of radius 40 m is banked so that tanθ = 0.25. Find the most safe speed. (g = 10 m/s²)
checks.hint: v_{s} = √(rg tanθ).

checks.q: A car travels on a banked curved road faster than the most safe speed v_{s}. In which direction does static friction act on the tyres?
options: Down the banked incline, helping provide extra centripetal force
Up the banked incline, opposing the inward pull
Static friction becomes zero above v_{s}
checks.hint: At speeds above v_{s}, the car tends to skid outward (up the slope), so friction opposes that tendency.
checks.explain: When v > v_{s}, the horizontal component of normal reaction alone is not enough, so the car tends to skid up the slope. Static friction acts down the incline so its horizontal component adds to the centripetal force.

checks.q: On a banked road with friction, if μ_{s} ≥ cotθ (for example θ ≥ 45° with μ_{s} = 1), the denominator of v_{max} reaches zero and there is no upper speed limit against skidding.
checks.hint: Look at the denominator (1 − μ_{s} tanθ) in the formula for v_{max}.
checks.explain: Since v_{max} = √(rg(μ_{s} + tanθ)/(1 − μ_{s} tanθ)), when μ_{s} tanθ ≥ 1 (i.e. μ_{s} ≥ cotθ), the denominator becomes zero or negative, meaning the vehicle will not skid outward at any speed (though it could topple).

stops.title: Conical pendulum
stops.inShort: The bob moves in a horizontal circle while the string traces a cone. tanθ = v²/(r g) and period T = 2π√(L cosθ / g).

cards.text: In a conical pendulum a bob of mass m on a string of length L moves in a horizontal circle, and the string sweeps out a cone of semi-vertical angle θ. The tension T_{0} is resolved: T_{0}cosθ balances mg and T_{0}sinθ is the centripetal force.
So T_{0}sinθ = mrω² and T_{0}cosθ = mg. Dividing, tanθ = rω²/g, where r = L sinθ. This gives ω² = g/(L cosθ).
The period is T = 2π√(L cosθ/g) and the frequency is n = (1/2π)√(g/(L cosθ)). The string can never become horizontal, since T_{0}cosθ must balance mg.

checks.q: A conical pendulum has string length L = 1 m and the string makes θ = 60° with the vertical. Find its period. (g = 10 m/s²)
checks.hint: T = 2π√(L cosθ/g). cos 60° = 0.5.

checks.q: On which quantities does the period of a conical pendulum depend?
options: L and θ (and g), but not on the mass m
checks.hint: Look at T = 2π√(L cosθ/g). Is m there?
checks.explain: T = 2π√(L cosθ/g) contains L, θ and g. The mass cancels out.

checks.q: If the bob is whirled fast enough, the string of a conical pendulum can become horizontal.
checks.hint: What would balance the weight if the tension were horizontal?
checks.explain: False. For a horizontal string, T_{0}cosθ = 0 and nothing would balance mg. Also θ = 90° would give T = 0, which is impossible.

stops.title: Vertical circular motion
sections: 1.4.1 Point Mass Undergoing Vertical Circular Motion Under Gravity
stops.inShort: Gravity changes the speed, so the motion is non-uniform. On a string: minimum speed √(rg) at the top and √(5rg) at the bottom, and tension at the bottom exceeds the top by 6mg. On a rod the speed at the top can be zero.

cards.text: In vertical circular motion under gravity, kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy keep changing into each other, so the speed is not constant. Only at the top and bottom does the resultant of tension and weight point towards the centre.
At the top, mg + T_{A} = mv_{A}²/r. For just completing the circle T_{A} = 0, so v_{A} = √(rg). Energy conservation over a fall of 2r gives v_{B} = √(5rg), and T_{B} − T_{A} = 6mg.
A rigid rod does not need tension at the top, so the speed at the top can be (practically) zero. For a rod the minimum speed at the lowest point is 2√(rg).

checks.q: A bob on a string of length 0.8 m is whirled in a vertical circle. Find the minimum speed at the lowest point so that the string never slackens. (g = 10 m/s²)
For a bob on a string in a vertical circle, what is T_{bottom} − T_{top}?
checks.hint: Subtract the equation at the top from the equation at the bottom, then use energy conservation.
checks.explain: T_{B} − T_{A} = 2mg + m(v_{B}² − v_{A}²)/r, and v_{B}² − v_{A}² = 4rg, so the difference is 6mg.

checks.q: For a bob tied to a light rigid rod, it is possible for the speed at the top to be zero.
checks.hint: Does a rod need tension to stay straight the way a string does?
checks.explain: True. A rigid rod can push as well as pull, so no minimum speed is needed at the top. A string needs v ≥ √(rg).

stops.title: Sphere of death and over-bridge
sections: 1.4.3 Vehicle at the Top of a Convex Over-Bridge
stops.inShort: In the sphere of death the rider needs at least √(rg) at the top. On a convex bridge, mg − N = mv²/r, so the vehicle leaves the road if v > √(rg).

cards.text: A rider going in vertical circles inside a hollow sphere follows the same dynamics as the bob on a string, with the tension T replaced by the normal reaction N. So the minimum speed is √(rg) at the top and √(5rg) at the bottom.
At the top of a convex bridge of radius r the weight and normal reaction are both vertical. The resultant is the centripetal force: mg − N = mv²/r.
As v increases, N decreases, and N = 0 marks the limit of contact. This gives v_{max} = √(rg); above this speed the vehicle leaves the surface.

checks.q: A convex bridge has radius of curvature 40 m. Find the maximum speed at which a vehicle can cross the top without losing contact. (g = 10 m/s²)
checks.hint: At the limit N = 0, so mg = mv²/r.
checks.explain: At the limit N = 0, so v_{max} = √(rg) = √(40 × 10) = 20 m/s.

checks.q: A vehicle is at the top of a convex over-bridge of radius r moving at speed v. Which relation holds for the normal reaction N?
checks.hint: The centre of the circle is below the vehicle. Which force is larger, weight or N?
checks.explain: Taking downward (towards the centre) as positive, mg − N = mv²/r, so N = mg − mv²/r.

checks.q: In the sphere of death, the rider at the top with the minimum speed √(rg) has zero normal reaction there.
checks.hint: In the string case, the minimum speed corresponds to T = 0. N plays the role of T.
checks.explain: True. N replaces T, and just completing the circle means N = 0 at the top, giving v = √(rg).

stops.title: Moment of inertia
sections: 1.5 Moment of Inertia as an Analogous Quantity for Mass
stops.inShort: I = Σ m r² plays the role of mass in rotation, and rotational KE = ½ I ω². Ring: I = MR². Disc: I = ½ MR². Radius of gyration K is defined by I = MK².

cards.text: Moment of inertia I = Σ m_{i}r_{i}² is the rotational analogue of mass. It depends on the mass and on how it is spread about the axis. The SI unit is kg m² and the dimensions are [M¹L²T⁰]. Rotational KE = ½Iω².
For a uniform ring of mass M and radius R about its own axis (perpendicular to its plane through the centre), I = MR². For a uniform disc about the same kind of axis, I = ½MR².
The radius of gyration K is defined by I = MK². It is the distance from the axis at which the whole mass could sit to give the same I. A larger K means the mass is farther from the axis.

checks.q: A thin uniform rod of mass 3 kg and length 2 m rotates about an axis perpendicular to its length through its centre (I = ML²/12). Find its radius of gyration K (to 2 decimal places).
checks.hint: First find I = ML²/12, then use K = √(I/M) = L/√12.
checks.explain: I = ML²/12 = (3 × 4)/12 = 1 kg m². Radius of gyration K = √(I/M) = √(1/3) ≈ 0.58 m.

checks.q: A ring and a disc have the same mass and radius. About their own axes, which has the larger moment of inertia?
options: It depends on the thickness only
checks.hint: Compare MR² with ½MR².
checks.explain: I_{ring} = MR² and I_{disc} = ½MR². The ring has all its mass at distance R, so its I is larger.

checks.q: The radius of gyration K is the distance of the centre of mass from the axis of rotation.
checks.hint: K is defined through I = MK².
checks.explain: False. K is defined by I = MK²: the distance at which all the mass could be placed to give the same moment of inertia. It is not simply the position of the centre of mass.

stops.title: Parallel and perpendicular axes
sections: 1.7 Theorems of Parallel and Perpendicular Axes
stops.inShort: Parallel axes: I = Ic + Mh², where Ic is about a parallel axis through the centre of mass. Perpendicular axes (flat bodies only): Iz = Ix + Iy.

cards.text: I = I_{c} + Mh². Here I_{c} is the moment of inertia about an axis through the centre of mass, and I is that about a parallel axis at perpendicular distance h. M is the mass of the body.
For a laminar (flat, plane) body, I_{z} = I_{x} + I_{y}. The x and y axes lie in the plane of the body and meet at a point, and the z axis is perpendicular to the plane through that point.
A ring has I_{z} = MR² about its own axis. By symmetry I_{x} = I_{y}, so MR² = 2I_{x} and the moment of inertia about a diameter is ½MR².

checks.q: A body of mass 4 kg has I_{c} = 2 kg m² about an axis through its centre of mass. Find I about a parallel axis 0.5 m away.
checks.hint: I = I_{c} + Mh².

checks.q: Which relation is the theorem of perpendicular axes for a flat body?
checks.hint: The axes x and y are in the plane; z is perpendicular to it.
checks.explain: For a laminar body I_{z} = I_{x} + I_{y}. The first option is the parallel axes theorem.

checks.q: The theorem of perpendicular axes can be applied to any three-dimensional body, such as a solid sphere.
checks.hint: Remember the word 'laminar'.
checks.explain: False. It holds only for laminar (flat, plane) bodies.

stops.title: Angular momentum and torque
sections: 1.8.1 Angular Momentum in Terms of Moment of Inertia
1.9 Torque in Terms of Moment of Inertia
stops.inShort: Angular momentum L = r × p, which for a rigid body is L = Iω. Torque τ = Iα is the rotational form of F = ma.

cards.text: Angular momentum is the moment of linear momentum, L = r × p. Its magnitude is L = pr sinθ, and for a particle moving in a circle of radius r it is L = mvr.
For a rigid body turning about a fixed axis, adding m_{i}r_{i}²ω over all particles gives L = Iω. It is the analogue of p = mv, with I in place of m.
Torque τ = Iα is the analogue of F = ma. For a constant torque, rotational work is W = τθ and power is P = τω.

checks.q: A flywheel of moment of inertia 4 kg m² rotates at a constant angular velocity of 5 rad/s. Find its angular momentum L.
checks.hint: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, L = Iω.
checks.explain: L = Iω = 4 × 5 = 20 kg m²/s.

checks.q: A torque of 10 N m acts on a body whose moment of inertia is 2 kg m². Find its angular acceleration.
checks.hint: Use τ = Iα.
checks.explain: α = τ/I = 10/2 = 5 rad/s².

checks.q: L = Iω and τ = Iα are the rotational analogues of p = mv and F = ma, with moment of inertia replacing mass.
checks.hint: Match each rotational quantity with its translational partner.
checks.explain: True. Moment of inertia I plays the role of mass in rotational motion.

stops.title: Conservation of angular momentum
stops.inShort: With no external torque, Iω stays constant. A dancer pulling in her arms lowers I, so ω rises.

cards.text: Differentiating L = r × p gives dL/dt = r × F = τ, the net external torque. If the net external torque is zero, dL/dt = 0, so angular momentum is constant: Iω = constant, or I_{1}ω_{1} = I_{2}ω_{2}.
If the moment of inertia of a system decreases without an external torque, ω increases in the same proportion. A dancer pulling in her arms spins faster.
Since ω = 2πn, the law can also be written I_{1}n_{1} = I_{2}n_{2}. This is convenient when speeds are given in rpm or rps.

checks.q: A skater with moment of inertia 3 kg m² spins at 2 revolutions per second. She pulls in her arms so that I becomes 1.5 kg m². Find her new frequency.
A diver jumps off a springboard and tucks her knees tightly to her chest mid-air. What happens to her moment of inertia I and angular speed ω?
options: Both I and ω stay unchanged
checks.hint: No external torque acts mid-air, so Iω stays constant.
checks.explain: Pulling limbs closer to the axis reduces moment of inertia I. Since angular momentum L = Iω is conserved, angular speed ω increases, letting the diver complete more somersaults.

checks.q: When a spinning ice skater pulls her arms inward with no external torque, her angular momentum stays constant while her rotational kinetic energy increases.
checks.hint: Write rotational KE in terms of conserved L: KE = L² / (2I).
checks.explain: Because L = Iω is constant and KE = L²/(2I), decreasing I increases rotational kinetic energy. The extra energy comes from internal muscular work done by the skater.

stops.title: Rolling motion
sections: 1.11.1 Pure Rolling Down an Inclined Plane
stops.inShort: Rolling = translation + rotation, with KE = ½Mv²(1 + K²/R²). Down an incline: a = g sinθ / (1 + K²/R²), so bodies with smaller K²/R² reach the bottom first.

cards.text: In pure rolling the centre of mass moves with speed v while the body rotates with ω = v/R. The body therefore has translational and rotational kinetic energy. Static friction is needed so that it does not slide.
Total KE = ½Mv² + ½Iω². With I = MK² and ω = v/R this becomes ½Mv²(1 + K²/R²).
For a body rolling down an incline of angle θ, a = g sinθ/(1 + K²/R²). A smaller K²/R² gives a larger acceleration, so a solid disc (K²/R² = ½) beats a ring (K²/R² = 1).

checks.q: A uniform disc rolls without slipping down an incline of 30°. For a disc K²/R² = 1/2. Find its acceleration. (g = 10 m/s²)
checks.hint: a = g sinθ/(1 + K²/R²).

checks.q: A uniform solid disc rolls without slipping. What fraction of its total kinetic energy is rotational?
checks.hint: Rotational : total = (K²/R²) : (1 + K²/R²), with K²/R² = 1/2.
checks.explain: Translational = ½Mv², rotational = ½Mv² × ½, total = ½Mv² × 3/2. The rotational fraction is (1/2)/(3/2) = 1/3.

checks.q: A ring and a solid disc of equal mass and radius are released together from the top of an incline. The ring reaches the bottom first.
checks.hint: Compare K²/R² for the two: the smaller one rolls faster.
checks.explain: False. The ring has K²/R² = 1 and the disc ½, so the disc has the larger acceleration and arrives first.

stops.title: Chapter exercises
stops.inShort: End-of-chapter MCQs, short answers and numericals. Do these after all the stops.

cards.text: Keep these ready: v = ωr, F = mv²/r, v_{max} = √(μ_{s}rg) (flat road), v_{s} = √(rg tanθ) (banked road), T = 2π√(L cosθ/g) (conical pendulum), v_{top} ≥ √(rg) and v_{bottom} ≥ √(5rg) (string).
Keep these ready: I = Σ m_{i}r_{i}², ring MR², disc ½MR², I = I_{c} + Mh², I_{z} = I_{x} + I_{y} (flat bodies only), L = Iω, τ = Iα, I_{1}ω_{1} = I_{2}ω_{2}, KE = ½Mv²(1 + K²/R²).
Draw a free-body diagram first, decide which force is the centripetal force, then write the equation. For numericals, check units and that you used the correct axis for I.

checks.q: A uniform thin rod of mass 6 kg and length 1 m has I_{c} = ML²/12 about its centre. Using the parallel axes theorem, find its moment of inertia about a parallel axis through one end.
checks.hint: The distance from the centre to one end is h = L/2, so I = ML²/12 + M(L/2)² = ML²/3.
checks.explain: I = I_{c} + M(L/2)² = ML²/12 + ML²/4 = ML²/3 = (6 × 1²)/3 = 2 kg m².

checks.q: A metallic ring of mass 1 kg has I = 1 kg m² about a diameter. It is melted and remoulded into a thin uniform disc of the same radius. Find I of the disc about its own axis.
checks.hint: Ring about a diameter: I = ½MR². Find R² first, then use ½MR² for the disc.
checks.explain: Ring about a diameter: ½MR² = 1, so with M = 1 kg, R² = 2 m². The disc about its own axis: I = ½MR² = ½ × 1 × 2 = 1 kg m².

checks.q: A solid sphere (K²/R² = 2/5) rolls without slipping on a horizontal surface. What is the ratio of its rotational kinetic energy to its translational kinetic energy?
checks.hint: Compare KE_{rot} = ½(MK²)(v/R)² with KE_{trans} = ½Mv².
checks.explain: KE_{rot} / KE_{trans} = (½MK²v²/R²) / (½Mv²) = K²/R² = 2/5, i.e. 2 : 5.

board.text: State and prove the principle (law) of conservation of angular momentum.
board.answer:
Statement: When the net external torque acting on a rotating body is zero, its angular momentum remains constant.
Proof:
1. Angular momentum L = r × p.
2. Differentiating w.r.t. time: dL/dt = (dr/dt) × p + r × (dp/dt) = v × mv + r × F = 0 + τ = τ.
3. If net external torque τ = 0, then dL/dt = 0.
4. Therefore L = Iω = constant, i.e., I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂.

points.text: Statement: if the net external torque is zero, angular momentum stays constant
Proof: dL/dt = r × (dp/dt) = r × F = τ; with τ = 0, dL/dt = 0, so L = Iω is constant, i.e. I_{1}ω_{1} = I_{2}ω_{2}

board.text: A flywheel of a motor has mass 100 kg and radius 1.5 m. The motor develops a constant torque of 2000 N m. The flywheel starts from rest. Calculate the work done during the first 4 revolutions.
board.answer: θ = 4 × 2π = 8π rad. W = τθ = 2000 × 8π = 16000π J ≈ 5.03 × 10^{4} J (with π = 3.142, W = 50 272 J). The mass and radius are not needed.

points.text: Angle turned in 4 revolutions: θ = 4 × 2π = 8π rad
Formula W = τθ with correct substitution, W = 2000 × 8π
Final answer 16000π J ≈ 5.03 × 10^{4} J with unit

board.text: The power rating of a ceiling fan rotating with a constant torque of 2 N m at an angular speed of 2π rad/s is:

points.text: Correct option (d) 4π W

board.text: State the formula for the angle of banking.

points.text: tanθ = v²/(rg), i.e. θ = tan⁻¹(v²/rg)

board.text: Derive expressions for the linear velocity at the lowest position, midway position and topmost position for a particle revolving in a vertical circle, if it has to just complete circular motion without the string slackening at the top.
board.answer:
Consider a particle of mass m performing vertical circular motion of radius r tied to a string.
1. At the topmost position (A), for just completing the circle, tension T_A = 0.
   Thus mg = mv_t²/r  ⇒  v_t = √(rg).
2. From top (A) to midway position (B), vertical fall h = r.
   By conservation of energy: ½mv_m² = ½mv_t² + mgr  ⇒  v_m² = rg + 2gr = 3rg  ⇒  v_m = √(3rg).
3. From top (A) to lowest position (C), vertical fall h = 2r.
   By conservation of energy: ½mv_b² = ½mv_t² + mg(2r)  ⇒  v_b² = rg + 4gr = 5rg  ⇒  v_b = √(5rg).

points.text: Top, just completing the circle: T = 0, so mg = mv_{t}²/r
Midway (fall r): v_{m}² = v_{t}² + 2gr, so v_{m} = √(3rg)
Bottom (fall 2r): v_{b}² = v_{t}² + 4gr, so v_{b} = √(5rg)

board.text: If friction is made zero for a road, can a vehicle move safely on this road?
board.answer: Yes, only if the road is banked and the vehicle moves at the most safe speed v = √(rg tanθ). The horizontal component of the normal reaction then supplies the centripetal force.

points.text: Yes, only if the road is banked and the vehicle moves at the safe speed v = √(rg tanθ)

board.text: Derive an expression for the kinetic energy of a body rotating with a uniform angular speed.
board.answer: Each particle has v_{i} = r_{i}ω, so KE_{i} = ½m_{i}r_{i}²ω². Summing over all particles: KE = ½(Σ m_{i}r_{i}²)ω² = ½Iω². Draw a diagram of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis.

points.text: Each particle: v_{i} = r_{i}ω, so KE_{i} = ½m_{i}r_{i}²ω²
Sum over all particles: KE = ½(Σ m_{i}r_{i}²)ω²
Result KE = ½Iω², with I = Σ m_{i}r_{i}²

board.text: Define moment of inertia of a rotating rigid body. State its SI unit and dimensions.
board.answer: Moment of inertia is the sum of the products of the mass of each particle and the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation, I = Σ m r². SI unit: kg m². Dimensions: [M¹L²T⁰].

points.text: Definition: sum of the products of the mass of each particle and the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis, I = Σ m r²
SI unit kg m² and dimensions [M¹L²T⁰]

board.text: An electron revolves round the nucleus in a circular orbit of radius 5.3 × 10^{-11} m with speed 3 × 10^{6} m/s. Find its angular momentum. (mass of electron = 9.1 × 10^{-31} kg)

points.text: Formula L = mvr with correct substitution
Final answer 1.447 × 10^{-34} with unit kg m²/s

board.text: A bob performs vertical circular motion on a string. The difference in tension in the string at the horizontal position and at the uppermost position is:
board.answer: (c) 3mg. Reason: T_{top} = mv_{t}²/r − mg and T_{horizontal} = mv_{h}²/r. Also v_{h}² = v_{t}² + 2gr, so T_{h} − T_{top} = 2mg + mg = 3mg.

points.text: Correct option (c) 3mg

board.text: Calculate the moment of inertia of a uniform disc of mass 10 kg and radius 60 cm about an axis perpendicular to its plane through its centre.

points.text: Formula I = ½MR², correct substitution (0.6 m) and final answer 1.8 kg m² with unit

board.text: Obtain an expression for the period of a conical pendulum. State the factors on which its period depends.
board.answer: Resolve string tension T₀ into vertical and horizontal components: T₀ cosθ = mg and T₀ sinθ = mrω² (with r = L sinθ). Dividing gives ω² = g / (L cosθ), so ω = √(g / (L cosθ)). Since T = 2π/ω, the period is T = 2π√(L cosθ / g). It depends on length L, semi-vertical angle θ, and acceleration due to gravity g (independent of the bob mass).

points.text: Force balance equations: T₀ cosθ = mg and T₀ sinθ = mrω²
Substitute r = L sinθ and obtain T = 2π√(L cosθ / g)
State factors: length L, angle θ, and g (independent of mass)

board.text: State and prove the theorem of parallel axes for moment of inertia.
board.answer: Statement: The moment of inertia I_{o} of a body about any axis equals its moment of inertia I_{c} about a parallel axis through its centre of mass plus Mh², where M is the mass and h is the perpendicular distance between the two axes (I_{o} = I_{c} + Mh²). Proof: Take C at the origin and O at (−h, 0). For mass element dm at (x, y), I_{o} = ∫[(x + h)² + y²] dm = ∫(x² + y²) dm + 2h∫x dm + h²∫dm = I_{c} + 0 + Mh² (since ∫x dm = 0 about the centre of mass).

points.text: Clear statement and formula I_{o} = I_{c} + Mh²
Setup with element dm and expansion ∫[(x + h)² + y²] dm
Use ∫x dm = 0 about centre of mass to arrive at I_{o} = I_{c} + Mh²

board.text: Derive expressions for the linear speed at the bottom and linear acceleration of a rigid body rolling without slipping down an inclined plane of height h and inclination θ.
board.answer: By conservation of energy: Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Iω² = ½Mv²(1 + K²/R²), giving v = √[2gh / (1 + K²/R²)]. Along the incline of length s = h / sinθ, using v² = 2as gives a = v²/(2s) = (g sinθ) / (1 + K²/R²).

points.text: Energy conservation Mgh = ½Mv²(1 + K²/R²)
Linear speed at bottom v = √[2gh / (1 + K²/R²)]
Use s = h/sinθ and v² = 2as to get a = (g sinθ)/(1 + K²/R²)

board.text: Derive an expression for the minimum safe speed of a vehicle moving in a horizontal circle along the inner vertical wall of a well of death of radius r.
board.answer: The normal reaction N from the vertical wall supplies the centripetal force: N = mv²/r. To prevent sliding down, the upward static friction f_{s} balances the weight: f_{s} = mg. Since f_{s} ≤ μ_{s}N, we need mg ≤ μ_{s}(mv²/r), giving v² ≥ rg/μ_{s}. Therefore, the minimum safe speed is v_{min} = √(rg / μ_{s}).

points.text: Force equations: N = mv²/r and f_{s} = mg
Apply f_{s} ≤ μ_{s}N to obtain v_{min} = √(rg / μ_{s})

derivations.title: Speeds in a vertical circle (just completing the circle)
derivations.given: A particle of mass m is tied to a string of length r and whirled in a vertical circle. It just completes the circle, so the tension at the top is zero. Positions: A = top, C = midway (string horizontal), B = bottom.

steps.line: At the top: mg + T_{A} = mv_{A}²/r
steps.note: Tension and weight both point down, towards the centre.

steps.line: Just completing the circle: T_{A} = 0, so mg = mv_{A}²/r and v_{A} = √(rg)
steps.note: This is the minimum speed at the top.

steps.line: Top to midway the bob falls through r: v_{C}² = v_{A}² + 2gr = 3rg, so v_{C} = √(3rg)
wrong: Top to midway the bob falls through r: v_{C}² = v_{A}² + gr = 2rg, so v_{C} = √(2rg)
Top to midway the bob falls through 2r: v_{C}² = v_{A}² + 4gr = 5rg, so v_{C} = √(5rg)

steps.line: Top to bottom the bob falls through 2r: v_{B}² = v_{A}² + 4gr = 5rg, so v_{B} = √(5rg)
wrong: Top to bottom the bob falls through r: v_{B}² = v_{A}² + 2gr = 3rg, so v_{B} = √(3rg)
Top to bottom the bob falls through 2r: v_{B}² = v_{A}² − 4gr, so v_{B} = 0

steps.line: Check at the bottom: T_{B} − mg = mv_{B}²/r = 5mg, so T_{B} = 6mg, which agrees with T_{B} − T_{A} = 6mg
wrong: Check at the bottom: T_{B} + mg = mv_{B}²/r = 5mg, so T_{B} = 4mg
Check at the bottom: T_{B} = mv_{B}²/r = 5mg, so T_{B} − T_{A} = 5mg
steps.note: At the bottom tension is up and weight is down.

derivations.title: Kinetic energy of a rotating body, ½Iω²
derivations.given: A rigid body rotates with uniform angular speed ω about a fixed axis. Particle i has mass m_{i} and is at perpendicular distance r_{i} from the axis.

steps.line: Every particle moves in a circle with the same ω, so v_{i} = r_{i}ω
KE of particle i: KE_{i} = ½m_{i}v_{i}² = ½m_{i}r_{i}²ω²
Total KE = Σ KE_{i} = ½(Σ m_{i}r_{i}²)ω²
wrong: Total KE = Σ KE_{i} = ½(Σ m_{i}r_{i})ω²
Total KE = Σ KE_{i} = ½(Σ m_{i})(Σ r_{i})²ω²
steps.note: ω is the same for all particles, so it comes out of the sum.

steps.line: Σ m_{i}r_{i}² is the moment of inertia I of the body about the axis
wrong: Σ m_{i}r_{i}² is the total mass times the radius, MR
Σ m_{i}r_{i}² is the angular momentum L

steps.line: Therefore KE = ½Iω², analogous to ½mv² with I in place of m

derivations.title: Conservation of angular momentum
derivations.given: Statement: if the net external torque on a system is zero, its angular momentum is constant. Start from the angular momentum of a particle, L = r × p.

steps.line: Differentiate with time: dL/dt = r × (dp/dt) + (dr/dt) × p
dr/dt = v is parallel to p = mv, so (dr/dt) × p = 0
wrong: dr/dt = v is perpendicular to p, so (dr/dt) × p = vp
dr/dt = 0 because the particle's position is fixed

steps.line: Hence dL/dt = r × F = τ, the net external torque (F = dp/dt)
wrong: Hence dL/dt = r · F, a scalar product

steps.line: If the net external torque is zero, dL/dt = 0, so L is constant
wrong: If the net external force is non-zero, dL/dt = 0
If the torque is zero, L must be zero

steps.line: For a rigid body L = Iω, so Iω = constant, i.e. I_{1}ω_{1} = I_{2}ω_{2}
wrong: For a rigid body L = Iω, so I/ω = constant
For a rigid body ω stays constant whatever happens to I

derivations.title: Most safe speed and angle of banking
derivations.given: A vehicle of mass m moves on a road of radius r banked at angle θ. Friction is ignored. The only forces are the weight mg and the normal reaction N, perpendicular to the road surface.

steps.line: Resolve N: N cosθ is vertical and N sinθ is horizontal, towards the centre
wrong: N sinθ is vertical and N cosθ is horizontal
N is already vertical, so it needs no resolving

steps.line: Vertical balance: N cosθ = mg
Horizontal: N sinθ = mv²/r, the centripetal force
Divide the two equations: tanθ = v²/(rg)
wrong: Divide the two equations: tanθ = rg/v²
Divide the two equations: tanθ = v/(rg)

steps.line: Most safe speed v = √(rg tanθ); angle of banking θ = tan⁻¹(v²/rg)
wrong: Most safe speed v = √(rg/tanθ); angle of banking θ = tan⁻¹(rg/v²)
Most safe speed v = rg tanθ; angle of banking θ = sin⁻¹(v²/rg)

derivations.title: Period of a conical pendulum
derivations.given: A bob of mass m on a string of length L moves in a horizontal circle of radius r. The string makes angle θ with the vertical. The forces are the weight mg and the tension T_{0} along the string.

steps.line: Resolve T_{0}: T_{0}cosθ is vertical and T_{0}sinθ is horizontal, towards the centre
wrong: T_{0}sinθ is vertical and T_{0}cosθ is horizontal
T_{0} acts vertically, so no resolving is needed

steps.line: Vertical balance: T_{0}cosθ = mg
Horizontal: T_{0}sinθ = mrω²
Divide: tanθ = rω²/g. With r = L sinθ this gives ω² = g/(L cosθ)
wrong: Divide: tanθ = rω²/g. With r = L sinθ this gives ω² = g/(L sinθ)
Divide: tanθ = rω²/g. With r = L sinθ this gives ω² = gL cosθ

steps.line: T = 2π/ω = 2π√(L cosθ/g)

derivations.title: Angular momentum L = Iω
derivations.given: A rigid body rotates with angular speed ω about a fixed axis. Particle i has mass m_{i} and is at perpendicular distance r_{i} from the axis.

steps.line: Each particle performs UCM with the same ω, so v_{i} = r_{i}ω
Linear momentum of particle i: p_{i} = m_{i}v_{i} = m_{i}r_{i}ω
Its angular momentum: L_{i} = p_{i}r_{i} = m_{i}r_{i}²ω
All L_{i} point along the axis, so their magnitudes add: L = (Σ m_{i}r_{i}²)ω
wrong: The L_{i} cancel in pairs, so L = 0

steps.line: Σ m_{i}r_{i}² = I, so L = Iω, analogous to p = mv
wrong: Σ m_{i}r_{i}² = I, so L = I/ω
Σ m_{i}r_{i}² = I, so L = ½Iω²

derivations.title: Torque τ = Iα
derivations.given: A rigid body rotates with constant angular acceleration α about a fixed axis. Particle i has mass m_{i} and is at perpendicular distance r_{i} from the axis.

steps.line: Every particle has the same α, so its tangential acceleration is a_{i} = r_{i}α
Tangential force on particle i: f_{i} = m_{i}a_{i} = m_{i}r_{i}α
Torque of this force about the axis: τ_{i} = f_{i}r_{i} = m_{i}r_{i}²α
All torques are along the axis, so they add: τ = (Σ m_{i}r_{i}²)α
wrong: The torques cancel in pairs, so τ = 0

steps.line: Σ m_{i}r_{i}² = I, so τ = Iα, analogous to F = ma
wrong: Σ m_{i}r_{i}² = I, so τ = I/α
Σ m_{i}r_{i}² = I, so τ = ½Iα²

derivations.title: Acceleration of a body rolling down an incline
derivations.given: A body of mass M, radius R and radius of gyration K rolls without slipping from rest down an incline of angle θ. It falls through a vertical height h while moving a distance s along the incline.

steps.line: Rolling KE: ½Mv² + ½Iω² = ½Mv²(1 + K²/R²), using I = MK² and ω = v/R
wrong: Rolling KE: ½Mv² + ½Iω² = ½Mv²(1 − K²/R²)

steps.line: Energy conservation: Mgh = ½Mv²(1 + K²/R²)
wrong: Energy conservation: Mgh = ½Mv²(1 + K²/R²) + ½Iω²

steps.line: So v² = 2gh/(1 + K²/R²)
Distance along the incline s = h/sinθ, and v² = 2as (starting from rest), so v² = 2ah/sinθ
wrong: Distance along the incline s = h sinθ, so v² = 2ah sinθ
Distance along the incline s = h cosθ, so v² = 2ah cosθ

steps.line: Equate the two expressions for v²: a = g sinθ/(1 + K²/R²)
wrong: Equate the two expressions for v²: a = g sinθ(1 + K²/R²)
Equate the two expressions for v²: a = g cosθ/(1 + K²/R²)
steps.note: Without rolling (pure sliding, no friction) the factor is absent and a = g sinθ.
